I expect you may not know what gaming on the PC was like before around 2003 or so. Steam has been a godsend for PC gaming. Before them the primary means of finding games was brick and mortar retailers. And then you'd go home, install it, and have to search the entire friggin web for patches and other media. Often times the developers, wanting to save on bandwidth presumably, would not even host the patches on their own site but on third party sites (often behind registration walls and all other sorts of nonsense) leaving you to dig through these sites to finally find the patch - if you could. Often times the patches for older games were simply taken offline.

And DRM - oh boy, I think that's a big tell tale sign you weren't gaming pre-steam. Star Force, Securom, and other such absurd technologies that would not only root your computer but attempt to disable virtual disk software and then grind the fuck out of any CD/DVD while you're playing just to constantly make sure it's real. Whirrrrrrr.....whirrrrrrr.....whirrrrrr every 30 seconds. The DRM on Morrowind physically broke my DVD drive. The company response? Too bad. That was what prompted me to move away from PC gaming and onto consoles at the time.

And multiplayer match making? Again, no such thing. You'd have to go sign up for yet another third party site, like GameSpy, and then navigate their god awful interface just to be able to play your games online with others. The reason Steam actually caught on early was because of this. Even though back in the day Steam was really little more than a DRM platform for Valve's games, one thing it did provide was native and seamless matchmaking - and it was amazing.

And I'm also a developer. I looked into getting into independent game development back during that time. The average deal you were looking at? Around 30% royalties after costs. In other words you go to a publisher and provide them a complete game. They in turn market and sell it. Once 100% of their costs are covered (because you know, a developer spending years making a game has no cost), they then take 70% of all remaining revenue and give you the leftovers. The deal you get with Steam? Developers get about 70% of gross. And you're also free to sell your product off steam while providing steam keys, and take 100% of gross if you like.

Steam unlike most companies with huge marketshare has never been coercive. The reason they're popular is because they simply provide an awesome product for incredibly cheap.
